hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer Bitly from a written spec. Claude passed all nineteen checks, but my spec never said how to count the last thirty days.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of Bitly a marketing team needs. Short links on your own domain. A UTM builder that only accepts your agreed sources and mediums. QR codes, counted separately as scans. And click counts that leave out bots and link previews.

The core rule is counting. A visitor is counted only once on a link in thirty seconds. Link previews from Slack or LinkedIn, and other bots, are recorded but never counted. A QR code carries a small marker in the link, so a scan counts apart from a click. And no IP address is ever stored.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation and the link builder. Redirects and counting. Reports and exports. Then reminders, the weekly digest and safeguards. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. The Links screen shows five seed links, with three hundred and forty-two clicks on spring. The new link form previews the final URL, with every UTM tag in order, and its QR code. The link page charts the clicks, with twenty-five previews left out. The campaign report adds up four hundred and seventy clicks by source and medium. And the outbox holds the weekly digests and an expiry reminder.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all nineteen checks passed, along with one hundred and fifty-one automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed sixty-nine places where Claude had to guess. Sign-in was limited to the company email domain, but no setting held the domain. A one-time sign-in link could be used up by a link preview in Slack. And the source and medium fields could be dropdowns, which made the check that refuses f b impossible to try. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, the daily job on a real scheduler, a real short domain, or redirect speed under load. And the QR codes were decoded by software, not scanned by a phone camera.

So is it worth building? Billed yearly, Bitly's Core plan is ten dollars a month, Growth twenty-nine and Premium one hundred and ninety-nine. Changing where a link points is limited to five, twenty or one hundred and ten times a month, and multiple users are an Enterprise addition. If one person makes a handful of links a month, Core may be enough. If your team shares links and keeps changing where printed QR codes point, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, nine rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all nineteen checks, with the sixty-nine fixes already in.
